knowledge_point.title: Determining the Points Where the Tangent is Horizontal or Vertical

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is horizontal. Give exact answers.

In **ascending order**, the tangent to the curve is horizontal at $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is horizontal if ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)),\,{y}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)} & =-1 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)=-1 \\ t & =\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{7\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{3\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})]=-\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{3\pi }{4}}\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}(\frac{7\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{7\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})]=\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{7\pi }{4}}\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the tangent to the curve is indeed horizontal at $t=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ and $t=\frac{7\pi }{4}.$
